blocks.prompt: The Bear That Waits
blocks.text: A polar bear does not live in a forest. It lives on the sea. The sea at the top of the world freezes into ice, and the bear walks out onto it. That ice is where its food is. Under the ice swim seals. A seal must come up to breathe, so it keeps a small hole open in the ice. The polar bear finds the hole. Then it waits. It can wait for hours without moving. When the seal comes up, the bear is ready. No ice means no seals to catch.

3.title: The Bear That Isn't White
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8

blocks.prompt: The Bear That Isn't Really White
blocks.text: A polar bear looks white. It is not. Pull one hair out and hold it up to the light, and you will see that the hair has no color at all. Each hair is clear, and the thickest hairs are hollow inside, like tiny tubes. Light bounces around inside that thick coat and scatters back out at you, and scattered light looks white. Snow does the same trick. Snow is only frozen water, and water is clear too. Under all that fur, the bear's skin is black. You can see it on its nose, its lips, and the pads of its paws. The coat has two layers. Underneath is soft, dense underfur that traps warm air near the skin. Over the top are long guard hairs that shed water, so a bear can climb out of the sea and shake itself almost dry. Below the skin lies fat, sometimes as thick as your hand is long. A polar bear is so well wrapped that it can overheat if it runs too far.

answers: it has no color, it is clear

on its nose, its lips, and the pads of its paws

blocks.prompt: A Marine Mammal With Fur
blocks.text: Scientists do not file the polar bear with the bears of the forest. They file it with the whales, the seals, and the walruses, as a marine mammal. Its scientific name, Ursus maritimus, means sea bear. The label sounds strange until you look at where the animal actually spends its life. A polar bear's hunting ground is not land. It is the frozen surface of the Arctic Ocean. That surface is not solid. It cracks, drifts, opens, and freezes again, and the bear travels across it for most of the year. Ringed seals live in the water below. A seal is a mammal and must breathe air, so it scratches breathing holes up through the ice and returns to them again and again. The bear's job is to find one and wait beside it. This is called still-hunting, and it is mostly waiting. A bear may crouch by a single hole, motionless, for hours. The bear is built for the waiting and for the ice. Its paws spread almost as wide as a dinner plate, which spreads its weight across thin ice. The soles are covered in small rough bumps and short claws that grip like the tread of a boot. Its nose is extraordinary: a polar bear can smell a seal through three feet of packed snow. It swims well, paddling with its front paws while its back legs trail behind like a rudder. But it swims far slower than a seal. In open water, a seal wins every time. Take away the ice and the bear loses its platform, and the platform is the whole hunt.

5.title: The Bear That Isn't White
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Blubber can reach four inches thick

blocks.prompt: Ice, Fat, and Time
blocks.text: A polar bear's life is an arithmetic problem. Seals are made largely of fat, and fat is the densest fuel an animal can eat. A bear that catches enough seals in spring converts them into a layer of blubber that can reach four inches thick, and that blubber is not decoration. It is a stored season. It has to be, because the hunting does not last all year. As summer arrives, the sea ice breaks apart and melts back. The platform disappears, the seals become unreachable, and the bear is pushed onto land, where there is almost nothing worth eating. So it waits. A bear on shore in summer is not lazy. It is spending its savings, and it loses roughly two pounds a day doing it. When the sea freezes again in autumn, the bear walks back out and starts earning. Pregnant females take the hardest path of all. In autumn a female digs a den into a snowdrift and seals herself inside. She gives birth in the dark of midwinter to cubs the size of a guinea pig, blind, nearly hairless, and helpless. She feeds them on milk that is nearly one third fat while eating nothing herself. By the time she breaks out of the den in spring with the cubs behind her, she may have gone without food for eight months. Everything those cubs are made of came out of the fat she banked before she dug in. Now change one number. If the ice breaks up two weeks earlier and freezes two weeks later, the earning season shortens and the fasting season stretches. The bear does not get a vote in this. A thinner mother produces less milk, smaller cubs, and fewer of them that survive their first year. This is why researchers watching polar bears spend so much of their time watching ice. The bear is not really an animal that lives in the Arctic. It is an animal that lives on a schedule, and the schedule is being rewritten.

6.title: The Bear That Isn't White
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Ursus maritimus, named in 1774
Descended from brown bears; the hybrids are fertile
Guard hairs are hollow and carry no pigment
The fiber optic fur story was tested and disproved
Nearly invisible to a thermal camera
Listed as threatened under the US Endangered Species Act in 2008

blocks.prompt: Ursus Maritimus: A Brown Bear That Went to Sea
blocks.text: Genetically, the polar bear is a recent invention. It descends from brown bears, and the split was fast enough that the two species can still meet, mate, and produce fertile cubs where their ranges overlap. Estimates of the timing vary, but the polar bear is likely only a few hundred thousand years old. In that window, evolution took a brown, forest-dwelling omnivore and rebuilt it into something that hunts on floating ice: the head narrowed, the neck lengthened, the teeth sharpened toward meat, the paws widened into paddles, and the coat and fat thickened until the animal could sit in an Arctic wind and lose almost no heat. That last part is worth pausing on. Look at a polar bear through a thermal camera and it nearly vanishes. The bear is producing plenty of heat, but so little of it escapes through the fur that the animal reads as barely warmer than the snow around it. The visible parts are the eyes, the muzzle, and the breath. The fur itself is one of the most misreported things in nature. Polar bear hair contains no white pigment. It is clear, and the thick guard hairs are hollow. For decades a tidy explanation circulated in books and classrooms: the hollow hairs work like fiber optic cables, piping sunlight down to the black skin, which soaks up the warmth. It is a lovely story. It is also wrong. Physicists tested it and found that the hairs conduct almost no light along their length. What actually happens is far less exotic. Light entering the coat bounces off countless surfaces, scatters in every direction, and comes back out as white. It is the same reason snow, sea foam, and crushed glass look white while a lake, a wave, and a windowpane do not. The skin underneath really is black. Whether it helps the bear warm up is genuinely unsettled, since almost no sunlight reaches it through that coat in the first place. None of this engineering solves the animal's actual problem, because the polar bear's problem is not cold. It is scheduling. A polar bear cannot catch a ringed seal in open water; the seal is simply faster. It can only catch a seal that has to surface, and it can only ambush that seal from a solid floor. Sea ice is not the polar bear's home in a sentimental sense. It is the bear's tool, and it is a tool that arrives and departs on a calendar. Every extra week of open water is a week of hunting deleted and a week of fasting added, and the bill for that arithmetic is paid in cubs. This is why the polar bear became the animal on the poster. It is photogenic, it is enormous, and its decline traces a straight line back to a cause. But the poster has a cost. A species reduced to a symbol gets argued about instead of studied, and the argument tends to be about the symbol rather than about ringed seals, breakup dates, and the price of a lost week.
